## 6 Threats to validity

This section discusses the study’s threats to validity based on Wohlin et al.’s framework Wohlin et al. (2012).

### 6.1 Construct Validity

Construct validity refers to the extent to which the employed measures accurately capture the intended theoretical constructs. This study strengthens construct validity by using multiple complementary measures: (1) perceived learning experience, engagement, and realism, assessed using a structured questionnaire, and (2) elicitation performance, evaluated through blind expert assessment using the Bano et al. Bano et al. (2019) taxonomy and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 criteria (2018). This combination of subjective and objective measures enables triangulation and reduces mono-method bias.

### 6.2 Internal Validity

Internal validity threats refer to factors that may influence the observed outcomes beyond the learning approaches themselves. A potential threat arises from the selection of participants. Although participants were randomly assigned to conditions in Experiment 1 and exposed to both conditions in Experiment 2, individual differences, such as prior experience with requirements elicitation, familiarity with conversational AI tools, and varying levels of technical proficiency may have affected performance. To mitigate these effects, Experiment 2 adopted a within-subjects design, allowing each participant to serve as their own control and thereby reducing the impact of individual variability.

Another potential threat concerns Instrumentation. Standardized tasks, instructions, and time constraints were applied across conditions to minimize procedural variability. However, the use of different underlying language models, GPT-3 in Experiment 1 and GPT-4 in Experiment 2, introduces an instrumentation threat, as differences in model capabilities may have influenced outcomes independently of the experimental conditions. Accordingly, the two experiments are treated as independent studies, and results are reported separately rather than through direct comparison.

The within-subjects design of Experiment 2 may introduce order, learning, and fatigue effects Wohlin et al. (2012). Participants completing one condition first may have developed strategies or familiarity that influenced performance in the subsequent condition.To mitigate this, the order of conditions was counterbalanced across participants, with each condition presented first for a subset of participants and then swapped in the second session. Nevertheless, residual learning and fatigue effects cannot be fully ruled out.

### 6.3 External Validity

External validity refers to the extent to which the findings can be generalized beyond the experimental setting Wohlin et al. (2012).

Interaction of setting and treatment. The study was conducted with software engineering students in an academic environment, which may not fully represent professional requirements engineering practice. In addition, the domain and system specification used in the experiments were intentionally limited in scope to ensure experimental control, alignment with course objectives, and comparability between conditions. Although this supports internal validity, it may limit the generalizability of the findings to more complex, real-world elicitation contexts.

Additionally, the smaller sample size in Experiment 2 (19 participants) introduces greater sensitivity to variability and may reduce the precision of the estimates compared to Experiment 1 (50 participants). While the within-subjects design in Experiment 2 partially improves statistical efficiency by reducing inter-subject variability, the limited sample size may still affect the stability of the results. Therefore, replication with larger samples would further strengthen the robustness and generalizability of the findings.
